```{r packages}

# Install and load packages

pkgs <- c("ape", "phangorn", "phytools", "ggplot2", "cluster", "pheatmap", "tidyverse", "patchwork", "BiocManager")

bioc_pkgs <- c("DECIPHER")

all_pkgs <- c(pkgs, bioc_pkgs)

install_and_load <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    
    if (pkg %in% bioc_pkgs) {
      BiocManager::install(pkg)
    } else {
      install.packages(pkg)
    }
  }
  
  library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)
}

invisible(lapply(all_pkgs, install_and_load))



```

```{r files}

# Read in the sequences as a string set
sequences <- readDNAStringSet("Data/combined_sequences.fasta")

# Align the sequences
aligned_sequences <- AlignSeqs(sequences, verbose = FALSE)

# Convert the sequences from a string set to a matrix
aligned_sequences <- as.DNAbin(aligned_sequences)

# Read in the csv showing which sequences were found at which outlets
outlet_info <- read.csv("Data/sequence_outlets.csv")

```

#### <br>
## Pairwise Distances

### Pairwise distances are calculated, using the Jukes-Cantor model (JC69) to account for substitutions that are not directly observed.

Assumptions of JC69:
- All four nucleotide states occur at equal equilibrium frequencies
- Every type of substitution occurs at the same rate
- Substitutions at different sites evolve independently

#### <br>
*p*: Proportion of observed differences/p-distance.

#### <br>

$$
p = \frac{differing\quad nucleotides}{aligned\quad positions}
$$

#### <br>
*d*: Expected number of substitutions per site.

#### <br>
Relationship between *p* and *d*:

#### <br>

$$
p = \frac{3}{4}(1-e^\frac{-4d}{3})
$$

#### <br>
Solved for *d*

#### <br>

$$
d = - \frac{3}{4}ln(1-\frac{4p}{3})
$$

#### <br>

```{r pairwise}

# Calculate the JC69 distances

jc_dist <- ape::dist.dna(
  aligned_sequences,
  model = "JC69"
)

# Get a data frame of the distances between the first five sequences
as.matrix(jc_dist)[1:5, 1:5] |>
  as.data.frame() -> first_five

# Display as a table
cat("Table 1: First five rows of JC69 euclidean distance matrix of the sequences.")

knitr::kable(
  first_five,
  row.names = TRUE,
  align = "l"
)

```

```{r quick info}

# Find the pair with the largest distance
large <- which((as.matrix(jc_dist)) == max(as.matrix(jc_dist)), arr.ind = T)
large_id <- row.names(large)

cat("\n\nPair with the largest distance:", paste0(large_id[1], " and ", large_id[2]))

```

#### <br>

### Principle Coordinate Analysis (PCoA)

#### Goal:
To easily visualise patterns of similarity and dissimilarity while preserving the original pairwise distances as faithfully as possible

#### How it works:
- Uses a distance matrix
- Calculates coordinates for each sample along a set of new axes (principle coordinates)
- Order the aces to capture the distance structure of the data in decreasing order of amount
- Each axis has an association value that helps determine how much of the overall distance structure it represents (often expressed on plots as a percentage)
- Plotting the first two or three axes allows us to visualise relationships bbetween sampes
- Some distances may be distorted when the remaining dimensions are omitted

#### Interpretation:
- Each point represents a sample
- The distance between points approximate the original pairwise distances
- Axes do not usually correspond to specific biological variables
- PCoA calculates eigenvalues, which indicate how much of the distance structure is represented by each axis

```{r PCoA, fig.width=18, fig.height=8, out.width="100%"}

# Perform PCoA using the JC69 distances
pcoa_result <- cmdscale(
  
  jc_dist,
  k = 4,
  eig = TRUE
  
)

# Visulalise the results:

# Extract PCoA coordinates
pcoa_point <- as.data.frame(pcoa_result$point)

# Name the first ten coordinate axes
colnames(pcoa_point) <- paste0("PCoA", seq_len(ncol(pcoa_point)))

# Add outlet information
pcoa_point |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "Sequence") |>
  left_join(outlet_info, by = "Sequence") -> pcoa_df

# Calculate percentages from positive eigenvalues
eig <- pcoa_result$eig
variance <- 100 * eig / sum(eig[eig > 0])

# Plot PCoA1 against PCoA2
p1 <- ggplot(pcoa_df, aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, colour = Outlet)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PCoA1 (", round(variance[1], 1), "%)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", round(variance [2], 1), "%)"),
    title = "PCoA: Axes 1 and 2"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 24),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 20),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 18)
  )

# Plot PCoA3 against PCoA4
p2 <- ggplot(pcoa_df, aes(x = PCoA3, y = PCoA4, colour = Outlet)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PCoA3 (", round(variance[3], 1), "%)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA4 (", round(variance[4], 1), "%)"),
    title = "PCoA: Axes 3 and 4"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 24),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 20),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 18)
  )

# Plot the two plots to display the first four PCoA axes
p1 + p2 +
  plot_layout(guides = 'collect')

cat("\n\nFigure1: First four PCoA axes of the DNA sequences")

```


```{r}

percentage <- round(variance[1] + variance[2] + variance[3] + variance[4], 1)

cat("Percentage of the positive-eigenvalue variation represented by the first four PCoA axes", paste0(percentage, "%"))

```

#### <br>
## Cluster analysis using kmeans
#### <br>

The k-means algorigm:
- samples are assigned to (k) clusters
- the centre (mean position) of each cluster is calculated
- the samples are reasigned to the cluster who's centre is closest
- steps 1-3 are repeated until the assignments stabilise

This results in the minimisation of variation within clusters.

#### <br>
### Choosing the number of clusters

One significant disadvantage of kmeans clustering is that we are required to specify the number of clusters a priori. Silhoutte analysis is an approach to this problem. The silhouette width is a measurement of how well each sample fits within its assigned cluster compared to the other clusters.
+1: the sample is much closer to its own cluster than to neighbouring clusters
 0: the sample lies near the boundry between clusters
-1: the sample may be closer to another cluster than to its assigned cluster

A higher mean silhouette width generally indicates better-separated clusters. However, it should be treated more as a guide than a difinitive proof that a particular number of clusters is biologically correct.

```{r kmeans}

# Extract all 10 PCoA axes for clustering
pcoa_coords <- pcoa_df[, paste0("PCoA", 1:4)]

# Calculate Euclidean distances in the PCoA space
pcoa_dist <- dist(pcoa_coords)

# Perform k-means clustering with different numbers of clusters
k_values <- 2:10
mean_silhouette <- numeric(length(k_values))

for (i in seq_along(k_values)) {
  
  km_test <- kmeans(
    
    pcoa_coords,
    centers = k_values[i],
    nstart = 25
    
  )
  
  sil <- silhouette(km_test$cluster, pcoa_dist)
  
  mean_silhouette[i] <- mean(sil[, "sil_width"])
  
}

# Plot the results
plot(
  k_values,
  mean_silhouette,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  xlab = "Number of clusters (k)",
  ylab = "Mean silhouette width",
  main = "Choosing the Number of Clusters"
)

cat("\n\nFigure 2: Silhouette width based on number of clusters. 5 is selected as the most optimal number of clusters.")

```


```{r clusters}

# Select the number of clusters with the highest mean silhouette width
optimal_k <- k_values [which.max(mean_silhouette)]

cat("Optimak k: ", optimal_k, "\n\n")

# Rerun k-means using the optimal number of clusters
set.seed(26112026)

km_optimal <- kmeans(
  
  pcoa_coords,
  centers = optimal_k,
  nstart = 25
  
)

pcoa_numeric <- pcoa_df[sapply(pcoa_df, is.numeric)]

# Score cluster assignments
pcoa_df$Clusters <- factor(km_optimal$cluster)

# Get the means for each cluster
# axes_means <- list()

# for (axis in 1:4) {

#   axes_means[[axis]] <- aggregate(pcoa_df[[col_name]], list(Clusters = pcoa_df$Clusters), mean)

# }

ggplot(pcoa_df, aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, colour = Clusters)) +
  stat_ellipse(type = "norm",
                 geom = "polygon",
                 aes(group = Clusters,
                     fill = Clusters),
                 alpha = 0.1,
                 linetype = 0,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PCoA1 (", round(variance[1], 1), "%)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", round(variance[2], 1), "%)"),
    colour = "Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

cat("\n\nFigure 3: K-means Clustering of Sequences, coloured by cluster.\n\n")

```

```{r closest}

# Find closest sequence to average of each cluster and save for later
pcoa_df |>
  group_by(Clusters) |>
  mutate(dist_from_mean = sqrt((PCoA1 - mean(PCoA1))^2 + (PCoA2 - mean(PCoA2))^2)) |>
  slice_min(dist_from_mean, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select("Sequence closest to cluster mean" = Sequence,
         Clusters,
         "Outlet sequence located in" = Outlet) -> closest

```


#### <br>
## Statistics
### Chi-Square Test of Independence
#### <br>

$$
x^2=\sum_{i,j}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
$$

#### <br>
Where:
\u2022 $O_{ij}$ = observed count in row *i*, column *j*\n\n
\u2022 $E_{ij}$ = expected count under independence:

$$
\frac{row_{i}total\times col_{j}}{grand\quad total}
$$

\n\n\u2022 The sum runs over every cell in the table.
#### <br>


```{r chi}

# Create table with Outlet and Clusters
chi_table <- table(pcoa_df$Outlet, pcoa_df$Clusters)

# Run Chi-squared test of independence
chi_results <- chisq.test(chi_table)

chi_results

```

#### <br>
### Equivalent linear model
#### <br>
Poisson regression with interaction terms between the two sets of variables.

#### <br>


$$
log(y) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \beta_{2} X_{2} + \beta_{3} X_{2} \beta_{3}
$$

#### <br>

$$
H_{0}: \beta_{3} = 0
$$

#### <br>
$X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ represent the two categories in the model, and $\beta_{3}$ is a vector comprising two values, corresponding to the combinations of cluster and outlet variables. The null hypothesis is that all values in this vector are zero, and that there is no interaction between cluster and outlet.

The test involves a comparison of two nested linear models:
\u2022 A full model which includes the interaction terms between the two sets of variables
\u2022 A null model which excludes the interaction terms.

```{r glm}

# Convert data to data.frame
chi_df <- as.data.frame(chi_table)
colnames(chi_df) <- c("Outlet", "Cluster", "Freq")

# Full model which includes the interaction terms between the two sets of variables

full_glm <- glm(
  
  Freq ~ 1 + Cluster + Outlet + Outlet:Cluster,
  data = chi_df,
  family = poisson()
  
)
# Null model which excludes the interaction terms.
null_glm <- glm(
  
  Freq ~ Outlet + Cluster,
  data = chi_df,
  family = poisson()
  
)

# Compare the two models using Rao's test
compare_glm <- anova(null_glm, full_glm, test = "Rao")

```

```{r compare chisq}

# Create a contingency table of the results
summary_chi <- data.frame(
  
  model = c("chisq.test", "glm"),
  "Chi-squared" = c(chi_results$statistic, compare_glm$Rao[2]),
  df = c(chi_results$parameter, compare_glm$Df[2]),
  "p-value" = c(chi_results$p.value, compare_glm$`Pr(>Chi)`[2])
  
)

cat("Table 2: Chi-squared values, degrees of freedom, and p values using different models to test the association between cluster and outlet.")

knitr::kable(
  summary_chi,
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = "l"
)

```

#### <br>

Interpreting these results:

\n\u2022 Chi-Square Statistic: The value of ~70 is the discrepancy between the observed frequencies and the frequences one would expect if there was no association between cluster and outlet.

\n\u2022 Degrees of Freedom: The value of 28 was calculated from (number of rows -1)*(number of columns - 1)
P-Value: the p-value is extremely small, so we can reject the null hypotheses.

#### <br>
### Pearson residuals

These residuals identify the largest descrepancies between observed and expected counts, to indicate which cells contribute most to the chi-square statistic.
\n\u2022 Positive residuals indicate that there are significantly more sequences from the outlet in that cluster than other clusters, and vice versa.
\n\u2020 Large positive or negative residuals indicate strong deviations in the cluster of a sequence based on the outlet it came from.

```{r residuals}

pearson_residuals <- chi_results$residuals

cat("Table 3: Pearson's residals of chi-squared test of independence between cluster and outlet.")
print(round(pearson_residuals, 2))

```

#### <br>
### Contribution diagram

```{r contribution}

# Get observed and expected counts
obs_counts <- chi_results$observed
exp_counts <- chi_results$expected

# Calculate percentage contributions
cont <- (obs_counts - exp_counts)^2 / exp_counts

total_chi <- chi_results$statistic
perc_cont <- 100 * cont / total_chi

# Visualise percentage contributions with a heatmap
pheatmap(perc_cont,
         display_numbers = TRUE,
         cluster_rows = TRUE,
         cluster_cold = TRUE)

```

Figure 5: Heatmap displaying the percentage contribution to chi-square statistic of the interaction between which cluster and outlet each sequence is found in.

#### <br>

```{r from}

# Finding the outlet with the largest residual for each cluster
max_resid <- data.frame(
  
  Clusters = colnames(pearson_residuals),
  "Outlet most associated with cluster" = apply(pearson_residuals, 2, function(x) names(which.max(x)))
  
)

closest |>
  left_join(max_resid, by = "Clusters") -> closest_resid

closest_resid |>
  select(
    Cluster = Clusters,
    "Sequence Closest to Cluster Mean" = "Sequence closest to cluster mean",
    "Outlet of Sequence" = "Outlet sequence located in",
    "Outlet Most Associated with Cluster" = Outlet.most.associated.with.cluster
  ) -> sorted_resid

cat("Table 4: Sequence closest to cluster mean, outlet of sequences, and most associated outlet of each cluster.")

knitr::kable(
  sorted_resid,
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = "l"
)


```

#### <br>

I am selecting the sequences that are closest to the mean of each group as representatives.
